reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: Eosinophilia is defined by an absolute eosinophil count above the normal range, with hypereosinophilia denoting persistently very high counts; the degree and persistence guide the urgency of evaluation
A practical framework separates causes into reactive/secondary (allergy, parasites, drugs, malignancy) and primary/clonal (myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms) plus idiopathic disease

Worldwide, helminth infection is the leading cause, so travel and exposure history and stool and serologic studies are essential, especially before immunosuppression that could disseminate strongyloidiasis
In high-income settings, atopic disease and drug reactions are common causes, and a careful medication review can reveal the culprit
Hypereosinophilic syndrome is diagnosed when marked eosinophilia persists with evidence of eosinophil-mediated organ damage and no identifiable secondary cause
Cardiac involvement (endomyocardial fibrosis and thrombosis) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, so troponin and echocardiography are important in significant hypereosinophilia
The FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion defines an imatinib-responsive myeloid variant, making molecular testing pivotal because it changes treatment entirely

Corticosteroids are the mainstay for symptomatic reactive and idiopathic hypereosinophilia, but empiric anti-parasitic cover for Strongyloides is prudent before starting them where exposure is possible
Peripheral counts do not always reflect tissue eosinophilia, so organ-specific disease can occur with only modestly raised or normal blood counts
reference.pathophysiology: Eosinophil production and survival are driven principally by interleukin-5, along with IL-3 and GM-CSF. In reactive eosinophilia these cytokines are overproduced by activated T cells or tumour cells in response to allergens, parasites, drugs, or malignancy. In clonal (primary) eosinophilia, a genetic lesion in the myeloid lineage-most classically the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, or rearrangements of PDGFRB, FGFR1, and JAK2-produces autonomous eosinophil proliferation. A lymphocytic variant arises from an aberrant T-cell population secreting eosinophilopoietic cytokines. Tissue injury results from release of eosinophil granule proteins (major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein), reactive oxygen species, and prothrombotic and profibrotic mediators, damaging heart, lungs, skin, gut, and nervous system.
additionalDifferentials: Atopic disease: asthma, atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and eosinophilic lung diseases
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides
Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and reactive eosinophilia in solid tumours or lymphoma
Adrenal insufficiency and, rarely, HIV infection
additionalInvestigations: Repeat full blood count to confirm and quantify the absolute eosinophil count
Stool microscopy and relevant parasite serology, with Strongyloides testing before immunosuppression
Serum tryptase, vitamin B12, and IgE with review of medications
Molecular testing for FIP1L1-PDGFRA and other tyrosine-kinase fusions, plus marrow examination and cytogenetics when clonal disease is suspected
Troponin and echocardiography (and cardiac MRI if indicated) to assess cardiac involvement
Targeted imaging and biopsy of affected organs
redFlags: Cardiac involvement with troponin rise, heart failure, or intracardiac thrombus
Neurologic deficits, thromboembolism, or rapidly progressive organ dysfunction
Very high, persistent counts (hypereosinophilia) with systemic symptoms suggesting evolving organ damage
Features of an underlying haematologic malignancy such as splenomegaly, cytopenias, or blasts
reference.prognosis: Reactive eosinophilia usually resolves once the trigger is removed or treated. Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome outcome depends on organ involvement and treatment response; the FIP1L1-PDGFRA variant generally responds very well to targeted tyrosine-kinase inhibition, whereas untreated cardiac disease carries a poor prognosis.
pitfalls: Starting corticosteroids without excluding Strongyloides, risking fatal hyperinfection
Attributing eosinophilia to allergy without considering clonal or parasitic causes
Relying on blood counts alone and missing tissue eosinophilic organ damage
Overlooking treatable molecular subtypes by not sending fusion-gene testing
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause: withdraw culprit drugs, treat atopic disease, and give targeted anthelmintics for parasitic infection
Empirical ivermectin to cover Strongyloides before starting corticosteroids, to prevent disseminated hyperinfection
Tyrosine-kinase inhibition with imatinib for FIP1L1-PDGFRA and other PDGFR-rearranged clonal eosinophilia
Corticosteroids as first-line for symptomatic idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome, with steroid-sparing agents and anti-IL-5 biologics such as mepolizumab for maintenance
Monitor for and manage end-organ damage, particularly cardiac involvement with troponin and echocardiography, and treat eosinophil-related thrombosis with anticoagulation
Haematology referral for suspected clonal disease with marrow examination, cytogenetics and molecular testing
Urgent treatment when severe hypereosinophilia threatens the heart or other organs

valueTables.title: Diagnosis of chronic eosinophilic leukemia and hypereosinophilic syndrome

cells.text: Persistent blood eosinophilia of at least 1500/uL, increased marrow eosinophils, and myeloblasts <20% in blood or marrow
Exclude all causes of reactive eosinophilia: allergy, parasites, infection, pulmonary disease (for example hypersensitivity pneumonitis, Loeffler's), collagen vascular disease
Exclude primary neoplasms with secondary eosinophilia: T cell lymphomas, Hodgkin's disease, acute lymphoid leukemia, mastocytosis

Exclude other primary myeloid neoplasms that may involve eosinophils: chronic myeloid leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia with inv(16) or t(16;16)(p13;q22), other myeloproliferative syndromes and myelodysplasia
Exclude T cell reaction with increased IL-5 or other cytokine production
Diagnosed when all of the above are excluded and there is no evidence of a clonal myeloid disorder

Diagnosed when all of the above are excluded and the myeloid cells show a clonal chromosome abnormality or other evidence of clonality, with blasts >2% in peripheral blood or increased in marrow (but <20%)
